title: Disentangling policy effects using proxy data: Which shutdown policies affected unemployment during the COVID-19 pandemic?
summary_en: When governments imposed COVID-19 shutdowns in early 2020, which specific policies actually moved unemployment? Kong and Prinz exploit timing variation in US state-level mandates (stay-at-home orders, non-essential business closures, restaurant bans) and use Google search-trend proxies to disentangle which policy levers drove unemployment-claim spikes. The paper provides one of the cleanest early decompositions of the labour-market cost of pandemic policy bundles.
data_used: US weekly state-level unemployment-insurance initial-claim data, mandate-by-state-by-date timing of stay-at-home orders and business-closure rules, Google search-trend volumes used as proxies for unobserved policy intensity. Difference-in-differences with proxy-data adjustments.
policy_relevance: Direct relevance for Hungarian and EU pandemic-preparedness policy frameworks (BM Belügyminisztérium, EMMI, OOK): when designing future bundles of NPIs the labour-market footprint is largest from blanket business closures, far smaller from voluntary stay-at-home advisories. For Hungarian Ministry of Health / Belügyminisztérium contingency plans, this suggests preferring sector-targeted closures over blanket shutdowns when feasible.
